claim: ROR2 mediates noncanonical WNT5A signaling to orchestrate tissue morphogenetic processes.
source: The receptor tyrosine kinase ROR2 mediates noncanonical WNT5A signaling to orchestrate tissue morphogenetic processes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about ROR2 function, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Dysfunction of the WNT5A-ROR2 pathway causes Robinow syndrome, brachydactyly B, and metastatic diseases.
source: dysfunction of the pathway causes Robinow syndrome, brachydactyly B, and metastatic diseases
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine-rich (CRD) and Kringle (Kr) domains of ROR2 was solved.
source: We solved the crystal structure of the extracellular cysteine-rich (CRD) and Kringle (Kr) domains of ROR2
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental determination of the crystal structure with detailed methods and results.

claim: The ROR2 CRD lacks the signature hydrophobic pocket that binds lipids/lipid-modified proteins, such as WNTs.
source: the ROR2 CRD lacks the signature hydrophobic pocket that binds lipids/lipid-modified proteins, such as WNTs
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ROR2 CRD lacking the hydrophobic pocket suggests a novel mechanism of ligand reception.
source: the ROR2 CRD lacks the signature hydrophobic pocket that binds lipids/lipid-modified proteins, such as WNTs, suggesting a novel mechanism of ligand reception
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural observation in the abstract.

claim: The ROR2 CRD is required for WNT5A signaling.
source: we showed that the ROR2 CRD, but not other domains, is required and minimally sufficient to promote WNT5A signaling
evidence: This is demonstrated through functional complementation assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ROR2 CRD is minimally sufficient to promote WNT5A signaling.
source: we showed that the ROR2 CRD, but not other domains, is required and minimally sufficient to promote WNT5A signaling
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mini-ROR2 construct experiments shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Robinow mutations in the CRD and the adjacent Kr impair ROR2 secretion and function.
source: Robinow mutations in the CRD and the adjacent Kr impair ROR2 secretion and function
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: FZ is involved in WNT5A-ROR signaling.
source: using function-activating and -perturbing antibodies against the Frizzled (FZ) family of WNT receptors, we demonstrate the involvement of FZ in WNT5A-ROR signaling
evidence: This is demonstrated through antibody experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: ROR2 acts via its CRD to potentiate the function of a receptor super-complex that includes FZ to transduce WNT5A signals.
source: ROR2 acts via its CRD to potentiate the function of a receptor super-complex that includes FZ to transduce WNT5A signals
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: ROR proteins were originally identified as orphan receptors based on sequence homology to other RTKs.
source: Originally identified as orphan receptors based on sequence homology to other RTKs (hence the name Receptor tyrosine kinase-like Orphan Receptor)
evidence: This is a historical statement about the naming and discovery of ROR proteins.

claim: ROR RTK family plays a critical role in mediating noncanonical WNT5A signaling.
source: work over the past two decades has elucidated a critical role of the ROR RTK family in mediating noncanonical WNT5A signaling (Oishi et al., 2003; Mikels and Nusse, 2006; Ho et al., 2012; Green et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Canonical WNTs signal through β-catenin-dependent transcription to regulate cell proliferation and tissue fate.
source: Unlike canonical WNTs, which signal through β-catenin-dependent transcription to regulate cell proliferation and tissue fate
evidence: This is established knowledge about canonical WNT signaling.

claim: WNT5A signals noncanonically through β-catenin-independent mechanisms to induce cytoskeletal rearrangements and tissue morphogenetic changes.
source: WNT5A signals noncanonically through β-catenin-independent mechanisms to induce cytoskeletal rearrangements and tissue morphogenetic changes (Konopelski et al., 2023; Moon et al., 1993; Veeman et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Robinow syndrome is characterized by systemic tissue shortening defects, including dwarfism, mesomelic limb shortening, brachydactyly, genitourinary defects, cleft palate, and other craniofacial dysmorphisms.
source: a congenital disorder characterized by systemic tissue shortening defects, including dwarfism, mesomelic limb shortening, brachydactyly, genitourinary defects, cleft palate, and other craniofacial dysmorphisms (Person et al., 2010; Afzal et al., 2000; van Bokhoven et al., 2000; Bunn et al., 2015; White et al., 2015; White et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the clinical features of Robinow syndrome.

claim: A distinct cohort of ROR2 missense mutations cause brachydactyly type B (BDB).
source: a distinct cohort of ROR2 missense mutations cause brachydactyly type B (BDB) (Oldridge et al., 2000; Schwabe et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Several anti-ROR therapies are currently in various stages of development.
source: several anti-ROR therapies are currently in various stages of development (Rebagay et al., 2012; Kipps, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The extracellular region (ECD) of vertebrate ROR proteins consists of an immunoglobulin (Ig) domain, a Frizzled (FZ)-like cysteine-rich domain (CRD), and a Kringle (Kr) domain.
source: The extracellular region (ECD) of vertebrate ROR proteins consists of an immunoglobulin (Ig) domain, a Frizzled (FZ)-like cysteine-rich domain (CRD), and a Kringle (Kr) domain
evidence: This is a description of the domain architecture of ROR proteins.

claim: The intracellular region of ROR proteins includes a tyrosine kinase domain and a serine/threonine/proline-rich domain.
source: The intracellular region includes a tyrosine kinase domain and a serine/threonine/proline-rich domain (Minami et al., 2010; Green et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations describing ROR protein structure.

claim: Cam-1 may not act as a typical RTK and may instead regulate the spatial distribution of WNT ligands.
source: which raised the possibility that Cam-1 may not act as a typical RTK and may instead regulate the spatial distribution of WNT ligands (Kim and Forrester, 2003)
evidence: This is a hypothesis raised by previous work, supported by citation.

claim: ROR function in vertebrates requires other domains of ROR proteins, including the intracellular domains.
source: this function requires other domains of ROR proteins, including the intracellular domains (DeChiara et al., 2000; Oishi et al., 2003; Mikels and Nusse, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations, though the current study challenges this view.

claim: The CRD of the classical WNT receptor FZ interacts with the palmitoleate moiety of WNT ligands directly through a hydrophobic groove.
source: the CRD of the classical WNT receptor FZ interacts with the palmitoleate moiety of WNT ligands directly through this groove (Janda et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to structural work.

claim: Free fatty acids have been observed to interact with the FZ CRD in the same fashion as WNT palmitoleate.
source: Free fatty acids have also been observed to interact in the same fashion (Nile et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The CRD of Smoothened (Smo) binds cholesterol through an analogous hydrophobic pocket.
source: the CRD of the Hedgehog signal transducer and GPCR Smoothened (Smo) binds cholesterol through an analogous hydrophobic pocket (Byrne et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The ROR2 CRD was previously implicated in WNT5A binding.
source: Because the CRD of ROR2 was previously implicated in WNT5A binding (Oishi et al., 2003; Mikels and Nusse, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The ROR2 CRD shares a high degree of amino acid sequence similarity with the FZ CRD.
source: shares a high degree of amino acid sequence similarity with the FZ CRD (Xu and Nusse, 1998; Saldanha et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: It is assumed that the ROR2 CRD possesses a hydrophobic groove similar to FZ CRD via which it interacts with WNT5A.
source: it is assumed that it possesses a similar hydrophobic groove via which it interacts with WNT5A
evidence: This is a statement about a previous assumption in the field.

claim: The two domains (CRD and Kr) share an extended interface.
source: we found that the two domains share an extended interface
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure (Figure 1).

claim: Deletion of the Kr domain severely impacted the yield of ROR2 constructs.
source: Analysis of construct secretion revealed that deletion of the Kr domain severely impacted the yield of ROR2 constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The crystal structure of the ROR2 CRD-Kr tandem domain construct was determined at a resolution of 2.48 Å.
source: We determined a crystal structure of the ROR2 CRD-Kr tandem domain construct at a resolution of 2.48 Å via a platinum single-wavelength anomalous dispersion experiment coupled with molecular-replacement (MR-SAD)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to methods and supplementary data.

claim: The ROR2 CRD comprises 5 α-helices (α1–5) and a single β-sheet (strands β1 and β2).
source: The CRD comprises 5 α-helices (α1–5) and a single β-sheet (strands β1 and β2)
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Kr domain presents a characteristic lack of secondary structure, displaying a single β-sheet (strands β3 and β4).
source: the Kr domain presents a characteristic lack of secondary structure, displaying a single β-sheet (strands β3 and β4)
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CRD is stabilized by five disulfide bonds.
source: The CRD is stabilized by five disulfide bonds: one located between β1 and a loop extending from helix α2 (I), a second linking α2 and the loop preceding longest helix α1 (II), a third between helix α2 and the loop between helices α3/4 (III), a fourth between long loops following helices α2 and α3 (IV), and the fifth between helix α3 itself and the loop extending from α5 (V)
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Kr domain is stabilized by two disulfide bonds (VI and VII) that are found within the core of the Kr domain.
source: The Kr domain is stabilized by two disulfide bonds (VI and VII) that are found within the core of the Kr domain
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CRD and Kr domains form an associated structural unit.
source: Overall, the CRD and Kr domains form an associated structural unit (Figure 1B, right-hand panel)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A contact interface is observed between the CRD and Kr domains and is dominated by van der Waals interactions, with two hydrogen bonds present.
source: A contact interface is observed between the two domains and is dominated by van der Waals interactions, with two hydrogen bonds present (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is described in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The domains share a small interfacial area of 559 Å2, with a reasonable shape complementarity score (0.7).
source: The domains share a small interfacial area of 559 Å2, with a reasonable shape complementarity score (0.7) (Lawrence and Colman, 1993)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: The structure of Kr in the CRD-Kr tandem domain closely resembles that previously described for the isolated human ROR1 and ROR2 Krs.
source: The structure of Kr in the CRD-Kr tandem domain closely resembles that previously described for the isolated human ROR1 and ROR2 Krs (Goydel et al., 2020; Guarino et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a high degree of structural conservation between the ROR2 and Nrk Kr domains.
source: There is also a high degree of structural conservation between the ROR2 and Nrk Kr domains (Shi et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Kr domains generally constitute protein-protein interfaces within multi-domain proteins.
source: Kr domains are generally observed to constitute protein-protein interfaces within multi-domain proteins (Deguchi et al., 1997; Ultsch et al., 1998; Zebisch et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work.

claim: The ROR2 Kr domain acts to stabilize the CRD.
source: suggesting that the ROR2 Kr domain acts to stabilize the CRD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of Kr impairs secretion.

claim: The CRD and Kr domains of Nrk also form an associated structural unit.
source: while the CRD and Kr domains of Nrk also form an associated structural unit (Shi et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The spatial arrangement of CRD and Kr in ROR2 is substantially different from that in Nrk.
source: the spatial arrangement of CRD and Kr in ROR2 is substantially different from that in Nrk (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CRD-Kr interfaces in ROR2 and Nrk are structurally distinct.
source: Correspondingly, the CRD-Kr interfaces in ROR2 and Nrk are also structurally distinct (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The full-length ROR2 ECD is monomeric in solution at concentrations as high as 48 µM.
source: The full-length ROR2 ECD is monomeric in solution at concentrations as high as 48 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C )
evidence: This is shown by SEC-MALS analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The CRD does not mediate dimerization as has been suggested for other related FZ-type CRDs.
source: indicating that the CRD does not mediate dimerization as has been suggested for other related FZ-type CRDs (Dann et al., 2001)
evidence: This is inferred from the monomeric state observed in solution, contrasted with previous work on FZ CRDs.

claim: The Ig and Kr domains do not facilitate oligomerization.
source: also suggesting that the Ig and Kr domains do not facilitate oligomerization
evidence: This is inferred from the monomeric state observed in solution.

claim: The CRD-Kr arrangement observed in the crystal structure is conserved in solution.
source: The CRD-Kr arrangement observed in the crystal structure is conserved in solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown by SEC-SAXS analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The N-terminal Ig domain is flexible relative to the CRD-Kr domain unit.
source: while the N-terminal Ig domain is flexible relative to the CRD-Kr domain unit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is shown by SEC-SAXS analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SAXS does not suggest that the ROR2 ECD forms a dimer in solution.
source: Additionally, SAXS does not suggest that the ROR2 ECD forms a dimer in solution
evidence: This is stated based on SAXS analysis.

claim: The TM helix and/or the intracellular domain could mediate dimerization of ROR2.
source: however, we cannot exclude the possibility that the TM helix and/or the intracellular domain could mediate dimerization
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the ECD is monomeric.

claim: The ROR2 CRD is evolutionarily related to other FZ-type 'groove-containing' CRDs.
source: Structurally, the ROR2 CRD is evolutionarily related to other FZ-type 'groove-containing' CRDs (Nachtergaele et al., 2013), such as MuSK and FZ8 (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 2; Stiegler et al., 2009; Dann et al., 2001; Janda et al., 2012)
evidence: This is shown by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1D and supported by citations.

claim: The ROR2 CRD is structurally distinct from 'pocket-type' CRDs such as NPC1 and RFBP.
source: These are structurally distinct to the 'pocket-type' CRDs such as NPC1 and RFBP, which bury their physiological ligands in deep cavities (Bazan and de Sauvage, 2009)
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous structural classification work.

claim: The FZ-type CRDs from both FZ8 and Smo exhibit shallow hydrophobic grooves for the binding of palmitoleate or cholesterol, respectively.
source: The FZ-type CRDs from both FZ8 and Smo exhibit shallow hydrophobic grooves for the binding of palmitoleate or cholesterol, respectively (Janda et al., 2012; Byrne et al., 2016; Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This is stated with citations and shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: FZ-type CRD grooves are structurally conserved when ligand free.
source: One general characteristic differentiating this subfamily of CRDs from the 'pocket-type' subfamily is that grooves are structurally conserved when ligand free (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B with citations.

claim: Minimal structural rearrangement occurs in FZ-type CRDs upon ligand binding.
source: with minimal structural rearrangement occurring upon ligand binding (Dann et al., 2001; Janda et al., 2012; Nachtergaele et al., 2013; Byrne et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work.

claim: The ROR2 CRD does not contain a visible hydrophobic groove pre-formed for ligand recognition.
source: Despite structural conservation with other FZ-type receptors, the ROR2 CRD does not contain a visible hydrophobic groove pre-formed for ligand recognition (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ROR2 CRD has evolved an additional helical insertion (α5) relative to the FZ8 CRD.
source: A structure-based sequence alignment shows that the ROR2 CRD has evolved an additional helical insertion (α5) relative to the FZ8 CRD (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The helical insertion (α5) in ROR2 CRD blocks exposure of any possible palmitoleate-binding groove.
source: Structural superposition of the ROR2 CRD with the FZ8:WNT-palmitoleate binary complex (Janda et al., 2012) shows that this helical insertion blocks exposure of any possible palmitoleate-binding groove (Figure 2F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: The ROR2 CRD structure is incompatible with a direct binding event occurring between the ROR2 CRD and the WNT5A palmitoleate moiety.
source: This observation is therefore incompatible with a direct binding event occurring between the ROR2 CRD and the WNT5A palmitoleate moiety
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that the groove is blocked.

claim: The high affinity 'site 1' WNT5A interaction must occur either via a different site on the CRD or through a separate co-receptor(s), or require structural rearrangements.
source: suggesting that the high affinity 'site 1' WNT5A interaction must occur either via a different site on the CRD or through a separate co-receptor(s), or require structural rearrangements as-yet not observed for groove-containing FZ-CRDs
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observation.

claim: The structure of the Nrk CRD revealed a deeply buried fatty acid.
source: The structure of the Nrk CRD revealed a deeply buried fatty acid (Shi et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: No bound lipid, nor an internal space that could potentially accommodate it, was observed in the human ROR2 CRD structure.
source: whereas no bound lipid, nor an internal space that could potentially accommodate it, was observed in our human ROR2 CRD structure (Figure 2D and F)
evidence: This is stated based on the structural analysis shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: The region of Nrk that interacts with the lipid does not superpose well with the analogous region in ROR2.
source: Structural comparison of the ROR2 and Nrk CRDs showed that the region of Nrk that interacts with the lipid does not superpose well with the analogous region in ROR2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residue K170 of Nrk that interacts with the head group of the fatty acid is absent in ROR2.
source: Notably, residue K170 of Nrk that interacts with the head group of the fatty acid is absent in ROR2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: R179 in Nrk is conserved in ROR2 (R280), but its side chain protrudes into solution.
source: Another basic side chain that contacts the head group of the lipid in Nrk is R179 – this residue is conserved in ROR2 (R280), but its side chain protrudes into solution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In FZ-CRD structures for which apo- and lipid-bound structures are available, major structural rearrangements within the CRD are not observed upon ligand recognition.
source: It is noteworthy that in FZ-CRD structures for which apo- and lipid-bound structures are available (e.g. FZ4), major structural rearrangements within the CRD are not observed upon ligand recognition (Shen et al., 2015; DeBruine et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work.

claim: ROR2 is unlikely to bind an internally buried free fatty acid analogous to that observed in Nrk.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that ROR2 is unlikely to bind an internally buried free fatty acid analogous to that observed in Nrk
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparisons.

claim: Primary MEFs were isolated from E12.5 Ror1f/f; Ror2f/f; CAG-CreER embryos.
source: For these experiments, we isolated primary MEFs from E12.5 Ror1f/f; Ror2f/f; CAG-CreER embryos that carry conditional (floxed, or f) alleles of Ror1 and Ror2, as well as a CreER transgene driven by the ubiquitously expressed CAG promoter (Susman et al., 2017; Hayashi and McMahon, 2002)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system with citations.

claim: E12.5 MEFs are particularly responsive to WNT5A-ROR signaling.
source: E12.5 was chosen because we previously showed that MEFs from this embryonic age are particularly responsive to WNT5A-ROR signaling (Susman et al., 2017; Konopelski Snavely et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The MEFs were immortalized via Cas9/CRISPR-mediated ablation of the Tp53 gene.
source: To enable long-term genetic manipulations, we immortalized the MEFs (called iMEFs) via Cas9/CRISPR-mediated ablation of the Tp53 gene (Dirac and Bernards, 2003)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with citation.

claim: The GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter can be quantified in live cells via flow cytometry.
source: this regulation could be quantified using the GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter in live cells via flow cytometry (Konopelski Snavely et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The WNT5A signaling deficit in ROR KO cells can be fully rescued by the expression of an exogenous WT ROR2 construct.
source: this deficit can be fully rescued by the expression of an exogenous WT ROR2 construct (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ROR KO reporter cells without any ROR2 rescue still retained some basal WNT5A signaling activity.
source: Interestingly, ROR KO reporter cells without any ROR2 rescue still retained some basal WNT5A signaling activity, which remained dose-dependent with respect to WNT5A concentration (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Additional receptor(s) exist in ROR KO cells to transmit the WNT5A signal.
source: This observation indicates that, while ROR receptors play an important role in promoting WNT5A signaling, additional receptor(s) exist in these cells to transmit the WNT5A signal
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of residual signaling in ROR KO cells.

claim: The two ROR2 mutants lacking the CRD (∆CRD and ∆CRD-Kr) completely failed to restore WNT5A-induced degradation of the GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter.
source: Signaling analysis using the GFP-Pdzrn3 degradation reporter revealed that the two ROR2 mutants lacking the CRD (∆CRD and ∆CRD-Kr) completely failed to restore WNT5A-induced degradation of the GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The CRD is essential for WNT5A signaling.
source: These results thus established that the CRD is essential for WNT5A signaling
evidence: This is concluded from the functional analysis of domain truncation mutants.

claim: Only the CRD is indispensable for the core function of ROR2 in promoting WNT5A signaling.
source: indicating that only the CRD is indispensable for the core function of ROR2 in promoting WNT5A signaling (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B)
evidence: This is concluded from the functional analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Mini-ROR2 can substantially rescue WNT5A signaling.
source: Signaling analyses by GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter degradation and DVL2 phosphorylation showed that mini-ROR2 can substantially rescue WNT5A signaling (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The ROR2 CRD is required and minimally sufficient to support the function of ROR2 in WNT5A signaling.
source: This experiment, taken together with the truncation analysis, established that the ROR2 CRD is required and minimally sufficient to support the function of ROR2 in WNT5A signaling
evidence: This is concluded from the mini-ROR2 and truncation experiments.

claim: ROR2 cannot by itself function as the signaling receptor for WNT5A.
source: we postulated that ROR2 cannot by itself function as the signaling receptor for WNT5A
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional observations.

claim: ROR2 likely facilitates the signaling function of another receptor(s).
source: instead, it likely facilitates the signaling function of another receptor(s)
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional observations.

claim: Members of the FZ family, particularly the FZ1, FZ2, and FZ7 subfamily, are plausible candidates for co-receptors in WNT5A signaling.
source: Members of the FZ family, particularly the FZ1, FZ2, and FZ7 subfamily, are plausible candidates, as numerous previous studies have implicated them in aspects of noncanonical WNT5A signaling (Oishi et al., 2003; Bryja et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2010; Grumolato et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2012; Konopelski Snavely et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A human mutation in FZ2 was recently identified in RS patients.
source: Furthermore, a human mutation in FZ2 was recently identified in RS patients (White et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The binding affinity of WNT5A appears to be higher for the FZ2 and FZ7 CRDs than for the ROR2 CRD.
source: the binding affinity appears to be higher for the FZ2 and FZ7 CRDs than for the ROR2 CRD (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Despite lacking the hydrophobic groove, the ROR2 CRD can still bind WNT5A via a presumably lipid-independent manner.
source: This finding is consistent with our structural data and with previous binding studies (Oishi et al., 2003; Mikels and Nusse, 2006; Sato et al., 2010), and suggests that despite lacking the hydrophobic groove, the ROR2 CRD can still bind WNT5A via a presumably lipid-independent manner
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data and structural observations.

claim: F2.A IgG, in its bivalent form and in the absence of any WNT5A, strongly induced GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter degradation.
source: Surprisingly, we found that F2.A, in its bivalent IgG form and in the absence of any WNT5A, strongly induced GFP-Pdzrn3 reporter degradation, as well as DVL2 phosphorylation, in ROR cKO iMEFs, ROR KO iMEFs, and WT ROR2 rescued iMEFs (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bivalent IgG F1.C, which specifically targets the CRD of FZ1, similarly induced GFP-Pdzrn3 degradation and DVL2 phosphorylation.
source: An independent bivalent IgG F1.C, which specifically targets the CRD of FZ1, similarly induced GFP-Pdzrn3 degradation and DVL2 phosphorylation (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F2.A IgG has an EC50 of 0.30 nM for inducing Pdzrn3 degradation.
source: Dose-response analyses of the F2.A and F1.C IgGs showed that these antibodies are highly potent in inducing Pdzrn3 degradation, with the respective EC50 values of 0.30 nM and 7.0 nM (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The F1.C IgG has an EC50 of 7.0 nM for inducing Pdzrn3 degradation.
source: Dose-response analyses of the F2.A and F1.C IgGs showed that these antibodies are highly potent in inducing Pdzrn3 degradation, with the respective EC50 values of 0.30 nM and 7.0 nM (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At post-saturating concentrations, both F2.A and F1.C IgGs exhibited reduced activity.
source: Moreover, we observed that at post-saturating concentrations, both IgGs exhibited reduced activity (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The F2.A and F1.C IgGs might function by inducing FZ dimerization.
source: suggesting that they might function by inducing FZ dimerization
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response behavior.

claim: The monovalent Fab of F2.A lost the ability to induce signaling on its own.
source: we tested the monovalent antigen-binding fragment (Fab) of F2.A and found that it not only lost the ability to induce signaling on its own (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The monovalent Fab of F2.A acted as a potent antagonist of WNT5A-dependent pathway activation.
source: but instead, acted as a potent antagonist of WNT5A-dependent pathway activation (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The F2.A Fab blocks the WNT5A-FZ CRD interaction.
source: presumably by blocking the WNT5A-FZ CRD interaction
evidence: This is inferred from the antagonist activity of the Fab.

claim: FZs function as the signaling receptors for WNT5A.
source: Altogether, these data support a model in which FZs function as the signaling receptors for WNT5A
evidence: This is concluded from the antibody experiments.

claim: ROR2 acts through its CRD to enhance FZ function, possibly by promoting WNT5A-FZ interactions and/or FZ dimerization.
